caption:
Cementing their names in history.

The Artemis III crew is leaving their mark — literally. The astronauts recently signed their names on the hardware that will be inside their Orion spacecraft during their low Earth orbit mission, launching in 2027.

Image descriptions:

1. The Artemis III primary and back-up crew members pose for a photograph inside the Vehicle Assembly Building at @NASAKennedy. From left, @EuropeanSpaceAgency astronaut @Astro_Luca and NASA astronauts @Astro_FrankRubio, @AstroKomrade, @AstroAndreD, and @Astro_FarmerBob smile at the camera. They are all wearing blue flight suits.

2. @Astro_FrankRubio signs an interior center wall panel that will cover environmental control and life support system (ECLSS) components inside the Orion crew module. He is wearing a blue flight suit and blue plastic gloves.

3. @AstroKomrade signs an interior center wall panel that will cover ECLSS components inside the Orion crew module. He is wearing a blue flight suit and blue plastic gloves.

4. A close-up of @AstroKomrade signing the panel that will cover ECLSS components inside Orion crew module. The note is written in silver pen on a black panel.

caption:
In a class of their own

Hidden within this star-forming nebula (captured by our Webb telescope in one of its largest images to date) are strange objects called brown dwarfs. Generally less massive than stars and more massive than planets, they are neither. They form the same way stars do, but they never quite "ignite." Just how small are the smallest objects created by the star-formation process?
 
The brown dwarfs here are about twice the mass of Jupiter - the least massive brown dwarfs found to date. For comparison, brown dwarfs are typically around 13 to 80 times Jupiter’s mass. These are so small, their existence poses challenges to the theories of star formation.

Adding to their strangeness, one of these showed signs of a disk, suggesting small planets could form around an object that itself is only the mass of a planet.

Read more at the link in @NASAWebb’s bio. See comments for image description. 

Image credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, Kevin Luhman (PSU), Catarina Alves de Oliveira (ESA), Mahdi Zamani (ESA/Webb)
